slides.body: Five mistakes to watch for.

items: git commit records nothing, or records a commit that lacks a file. Root cause: git commit records the index, and the change was never added to it.
Believing that saving a file changes the repository. Root cause: editing files is invisible to Git until git add; .git held the same four files before and after the edit.
Expecting HEAD to hold the new commit ID after a commit. Root cause: HEAD names the branch; the commit moves the branch file, and HEAD follows only through that name.
Running git init in the wrong place. Root cause: git init creates .git wherever it runs; in your home directory it turns everything you own into one working tree, so give it a directory argument.
Expecting your hand-typed IDs to match the book. Root cause: in labs/shell the clock is real, and the commit ID depends on the time.

beats.text: You edit a file. You save it. Your editor shows the new line, your local test passes, and the build server, the shared machine that builds and tests the team's code, fails as if you had done nothing.
beats.tele: You edit a file. You save it. Your editor shows the new line, your local test passes, and the build server, the shared machine that builds and tests the team's code, fails as if you had done nothing.

beats.text: Here's the fact behind that failure. A build server checks out a commit, one saved snapshot of the project. It never sees your working tree, and it never sees your index. Both get defined in a minute. For now: a change that was edited but not added, or added but not committed, doesn't exist for anyone else, however real it looks in your editor.

beats.text: git init creates a directory, not a connection. Recall the last video: the whole repository is the dot git directory at the top of your project. git init creates that directory. It contacts no server, creates no account and asks no permission, because Git has none of those things.

beats.text: One file, three places. A file you work on can be in three places, and the three commands of this video move it between them.
beats.tele: One file, three places. A file you work on can be in three places, and the three commands of this video move it between them.

beats.text: The first place is the working tree: the files you see and edit. Editing files is invisible to Git until you tell it.
beats.tele: The first place is the working tree: the files you see and edit. Editing files is invisible to Git until you tell it.

beats.text: The second place is the index, also called the staging area. It's one file, named index, inside the dot git folder, and it's the list of what the next commit will contain.
beats.tele: The second place is the index, also called the staging area. It's one file, named index, inside the dot git folder, and it's the list of what the next commit will contain.

beats.text: The third place is the repository proper: the objects in the objects folder and the names in the refs folder, both inside dot git. On screen the third box shows the last commit, which Git finds through a name called HEAD.
beats.tele: The third place is the repository proper: the objects in the objects folder and the names in the refs folder, both inside dot git. On screen the third box shows the last commit, which Git finds through a name called HEAD.

beats.text: What git add writes. git add does two things. It stores the content of the file as an object, one stored piece of data. And it records in the index which content belongs to which path. No commit exists after git add.
beats.tele: What `git add` writes. `git add` does two things. It stores the content of the file as an object, one stored piece of data. And it records in the index which content belongs to which path. No commit exists after `git add`.

beats.text: What git commit writes. git commit records the index. It writes the objects that describe the directories, called trees, and one commit object. Then it moves the current branch to that commit and writes a line in each of two journals, the reflogs.
beats.tele: What `git commit` writes. `git commit` records the index. It writes the objects that describe the directories, called trees, and one commit object. Then it moves the current branch to that commit and writes a line in each of two journals, the reflogs.

beats.text: The mechanism of "being on a branch". A branch is a name that points at a commit. HEAD names a branch, and the branch names a commit. That's the whole mechanism. A commit moves the current branch, and HEAD follows only because it names that branch.
beats.tele: The mechanism of "being on a branch". A branch is a name that points at a commit. HEAD names a branch, and the branch names a commit. That's the whole mechanism. A commit moves the current branch, and HEAD follows only because it names that branch.

beats.text: The risk labels. All three commands carry the label 🟢 SAFE in the textbook's command-safety table. git init creates the dot git folder, and in an existing repository it only adds missing template files. git add stores content as objects and points index entries at it. git commit adds tree and commit objects, moves the current branch, and appends to the reflogs. Each one only adds.
beats.tele: The risk labels. Each one only adds.

beats.text: Picture three boxes in a row: working tree, index, repository. A file starts in the left box. git add copies its content to the middle box. git commit records the middle box into the right box.
beats.tele: Picture three boxes in a row: working tree, index, repository. A file starts in the left box. `git add` copies its content to the middle box. `git commit` records the middle box into the right box.

beats.text: Notice the word "copies". After git add, the content is in the working tree and in the index. After git commit, it's in all three. Nothing leaves a box when it enters the next one.

It tells you where content is, and it says nothing yet about how the right-hand box is organized: what a commit is made of, and why a second commit doesn't store an unchanged file again. You'll see that the object count hints at an answer. The full answer is Part 1.

The two arrows underneath are the two commands: git add carries content from the working tree to the index, and git commit records the index in the repository.

beats.text: Five mistakes to watch for.
beats.tele: Five mistakes to watch for.

beats.text: git commit records nothing, or records a commit that lacks a file. Root cause: git commit records the index, and the change was never added to it.
beats.tele: `git commit` records nothing, or records a commit that lacks a file. Root cause: `git commit` records the index, and the change was never added to it.

beats.text: Believing that saving a file changes the repository. Root cause: editing files is invisible to Git until git add; .git held the same four files before and after the edit.
beats.tele: Believing that saving a file changes the repository. Root cause: editing files is invisible to Git until `git add`; `.git` held the same four files before and after the edit.

beats.text: Expecting HEAD to hold the new commit ID after a commit. Root cause: HEAD names the branch; the commit moves the branch file, and HEAD follows only through that name.
beats.tele: Expecting HEAD to hold the new commit ID after a commit. Root cause: HEAD names the branch; the commit moves the branch file, and HEAD follows only through that name.

beats.text: Running git init in the wrong place. Root cause: git init creates .git wherever it runs; in your home directory it turns everything you own into one working tree, so give it a directory argument.
beats.tele: Running `git init` in the wrong place. Root cause: `git init` creates `.git` wherever it runs; in your home directory it turns everything you own into one working tree, so give it a directory argument.

beats.text: Expecting your hand-typed IDs to match the book. Root cause: in labs/shell the clock is real, and the commit ID depends on the time.

beats.text: Let's land this. You should now be able to say: git init creates a .git directory with a HEAD that names an unborn branch, and nothing else of substance. Editing a file changes nothing under .git. git add writes the content as an object and writes the index. git commit writes tree and commit objects, creates or moves the branch ref, and appends to the reflogs.
